reasons: Lake identity gives case_name "United States v. Banks", court "U.S. Supreme Court", date_decided "2003-12-02", and year 2003.
Lake citations list official "540 U.S. 31", parallel cites "124 S. Ct. 521" and "157 L. Ed. 2d 343", and vendor-neutral cite "2003 U.S. LEXIS 8966".
The opinion is centrally about knock-and-announce timing: "The question is whether their 15-to-20-second wait before a forcible entry satisfied the Fourth Amendment and 18 U. S. C. §3109."

The opinion expressly builds from Wilson and Richards knock-and-announce doctrine, stating that Wilson made the common-law knock-and-announce principle a focus of reasonableness and that Richards supplied the reasonable-suspicion exigency exception.
residual_risks: No separate corpus taxonomy defining the exact role label "Progeny" is disclosed; this verdict treats it as a follow-on/application role within the Knock-and-Announce topic.

reasons: The opinion states: "We hold that it did" as to whether the 15-to-20-second wait before forcible entry satisfied the Fourth Amendment and §3109.

The opinion states that after 15 or 20 seconds police could fairly suspect cocaine would be gone if they waited longer, and that "it is imminent disposal, not travel time to the entrance, that governs when the police may reasonably enter."
The holding is limited to a felony drug warrant/easily disposable evidence context, matching the opinion's repeated focus on cocaine and the risk of disposal.
residual_risks: Banks stresses totality of the circumstances and calls the timing issue close, so the holding should not be read as a categorical 15-to-20-second rule for every drug warrant.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: Add "on these facts" or "where officers reasonably suspect imminent disposal of easily disposable drugs" to make the fact-specific limit unmistakable.
